title: Quiz: Process Capability Analysis — Cp and Cpk

questions.text: A process has USL = 110, LSL = 90, μ = 100, σ = 3. What is Cp?
questions.explanation: Cp = (USL − LSL) / 6σ = (110 − 90) / (6 × 3) = 20/18 = 1.11. Cp measures the ratio of the spec width to the natural process spread (6σ).

questions.text: Using the same process (USL=110, LSL=90, μ=100, σ=3), what is Cpk?
options: All of the above — they are the same
questions.explanation: Cpk = min((USL−μ)/3σ, (μ−LSL)/3σ) = min(10/9, 10/9) = 1.11. Since μ=100 is exactly centred, Cp = Cpk = 1.11.

questions.text: It is valid to perform process capability analysis on an unstable (out-of-control) process.
questions.explanation: Process capability analysis assumes the process is in statistical control (stable). Calculating Cp/Cpk on an unstable process gives misleading results — the control chart must confirm stability first.

questions.text: A process has Cp = 1.60 but Cpk = 0.90. The best immediate action is:
options: Reduce process variation by upgrading equipment
Recentre the process mean toward the midpoint of the spec limits
Stop production — the process is not capable
questions.explanation: High Cp but low Cpk means the process is capable of fitting inside the specs but is off-centred. Simply recentring the mean (without changing variability) will improve Cpk immediately.

questions.text: A Cpk of exactly 1.00 means that the process produces approximately 2700 defects per million opportunities (DPMO).
questions.explanation: Cpk = 1.00 corresponds to ±3σ — a process centred at 3σ from the nearest spec limit. The area beyond 3σ in a normal distribution is about 0.0027, or roughly 2700 DPMO.
